claim: The majority of mammalian promoters are CpG islands.
source: The majority of mammalian promoters are CpG islands; regions of high CG density that require protection from DNA methylation to be functional.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about mammalian promoters.

claim: CpG islands are regions of high CG density that require protection from DNA methylation to be functional.
source: The majority of mammalian promoters are CpG islands; regions of high CG density that require protection from DNA methylation to be functional.
evidence: This is stated as a defining characteristic of CpG islands in the abstract.

claim: CG density alone is a minor determinant of the unmethylated state of CpG islands.
source: Modeling of this comprehensive dataset revealed that CG density alone is a minor determinant of their unmethylated state.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract, derived from modeling the experimental dataset.

claim: Transcription factor binding sites play a principal role in determining the unmethylated state of CpG islands.
source: Instead, these data argue for a principal role for transcription factor binding sites, a prediction confirmed by testing synthetic mutant libraries.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the abstract, supported by experimental data from synthetic mutant libraries.

claim: The method developed allows interrogation of methylation states of hundreds of sequence variants inserted at the same genomic site in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: To address this question in a comprehensive manner, we developed a method to interrogate methylation states of hundreds of sequence variants inserted at the same genomic site in mouse embryonic stem cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental method developed and used in the study.

claim: In mammals, methylation of DNA occurs mainly at cytosines lying in a CG context.
source: In mammals, methylation of DNA occurs mainly at cytosines lying in a CG context and its presence correlates with transcriptionally repressed states (Deaton and Bird, 2011; Jones, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: DNA methylation presence correlates with transcriptionally repressed states.
source: In mammals, methylation of DNA occurs mainly at cytosines lying in a CG context and its presence correlates with transcriptionally repressed states (Deaton and Bird, 2011; Jones, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Unmethylated CGs are concentrated in regions that are unusually rich in CG dinucleotides compared to the rest of the genome.
source: Unmethylated CGs are concentrated in regions that are unusually rich in CG dinucleotides as compared to the rest of the genome (Bird, 1980).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation with a citation.

claim: Many unmethylated regions extend far beyond the CGI definition.
source: These datasets revealed that many unmethylated regions (UMRs) extend far beyond the CGI definition and that CGI can show variable levels of methylation (Meissner et al., 2008; Mohn et al., 2008; Doi et al., 2009; Hodges et al., 2011; Molaro et al., 2011; Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous methylation mapping studies with citations.

claim: CGI can show variable levels of methylation.
source: These datasets revealed that many unmethylated regions (UMRs) extend far beyond the CGI definition and that CGI can show variable levels of methylation (Meissner et al., 2008; Mohn et al., 2008; Doi et al., 2009; Hodges et al., 2011; Molaro et al., 2011; Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous methylation mapping studies with citations.

claim: CG poor regions outside of CGIs can have low methylation levels (Low Methylated Regions–LMRs).
source: Moreover, these studies identified CG poor regions outside of CGIs having low methylation levels (Low Methylated Regions–LMRs) (Hodges et al., 2011; Stadler et al., 2011; Hon et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2013; Ziller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies with citations.

claim: The recombinase-based targeting method yielded reproducibly up to several thousand integrants using a standardized transfection protocol.
source: This approach yielded reproducibly up to several thousand integrants using a standardized transfection protocol (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the method with reference to supporting figure data.

claim: The method generated unprecedented sequence diversity at a single genomic site in a higher eukaryote.
source: To our knowledge this generated unprecedented sequence diversity at a single genomic site in a higher eukaryote.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the method.

claim: 63.5% of tested sequences are methylated similarly to their endogenous counterparts despite only representing short sub-fragments of CGIs.
source: This analysis reveals that the majority (63.5%) of tested sequences are methylated similarly to their endogenous counterparts despite the fact that they only represent short sub-fragments of CGIs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing ectopic and endogenous methylation states.

claim: Elements as small as 100 bp were found to be sufficient to establish an unmethylated state.
source: For example, elements as small as 100 bp were found to be sufficient to establish an unmethylated state.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: 40% of the inserted fragments gained methylation relative to their endogenous site.
source: However 40% of the inserted fragments gained methylation relative to their endogenous site.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The frequency of CG explains only 14% of the observed variation in methylation (R = −0.37).
source: In fact the frequency of CG explains only 14% of the observed variation (R = −0.37), suggesting that differences in CG density between fragments contribute to a certain extend to their differential methylation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: At very high CG frequencies (≥12CGs/100 bp), CGs appear sufficient to explain an unmethylated state of small fragments after insertion.
source: Thus at very high frequencies, CGs appear sufficient to explain an unmethylated state of small fragments after insertion, while at lower densities numerous fragments of similar CG density show highly variable methylation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At lower CG densities, numerous fragments of similar CG density show highly variable methylation.
source: Thus at very high frequencies, CGs appear sufficient to explain an unmethylated state of small fragments after insertion, while at lower densities numerous fragments of similar CG density show highly variable methylation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Prokaryotic DNA is not under selection for binding sites for mammalian transcription factors.
source: This prokaryotic DNA is not under selection for binding sites for mammalian transcription factors, allowing us to measure the effect of CG density in an isolated context.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using E. coli DNA in the experiments.

claim: At the highest CG densities (≥12CG/100 bp), prokaryotic sequences remain unmethylated consistent with previous observations that CG density can protect prokaryotic sequences from de novo methylation.
source: Similar to the inserted mouse fragments the unmethylated state can be observed at the highest CG densities (≥12CG/100 bp) consistent with previous observations that CG density can also protect prokaryotic sequences from de novo methylation (Lienert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data with reference to a previous study.

claim: At lower CG density, prokaryotic sequences get readily methylated.
source: At a lower CG density however prokaryotic sequences get readily methylated, as revealed by higher average methylation and a significantly reduced spread compared to mouse fragments with similar CG content (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a much stronger negative correlation between CG density and methylation for prokaryotic fragments (R = 0.65) than for mouse fragments.
source: Moreover, we observe a much stronger negative correlation between CG density and methylation for these fragments than the mouse fragments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, R = 0.65).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis comparing the two fragment types.

claim: The 'CG only' model derived from prokaryotic sequences has predictive power for mouse fragments (R = 0.38).
source: This comparison reveals that the 'CG only' model indeed has predictive power (Figure 3C, R = 0.38), however numerous mouse fragments are significantly less methylated than predicted based on their CG content, arguing that additional sequence cues contribute to their unmethylated state.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the model to mouse fragments.

claim: Numerous mouse fragments are significantly less methylated than predicted based on their CG content, arguing that additional sequence cues contribute to their unmethylated state.
source: This comparison reveals that the 'CG only' model indeed has predictive power (Figure 3C, R = 0.38), however numerous mouse fragments are significantly less methylated than predicted based on their CG content, arguing that additional sequence cues contribute to their unmethylated state.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing predicted and observed methylation.

claim: Fragments that are unmethylated despite being predicted to be methylated based on CG content show significantly higher DNaseI hypersensitive (DHS) site enrichment.
source: Despite being predicted to be methylated based on their CG content, those fragments that are unmethylated indeed show significantly higher DHS enrichment (Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from analyzing DHS data at endogenous loci.

claim: Mutated sequences where all non-CG nucleotides are replaced by E. coli sequence display a strong shift in methylation states for fragments predicted to have weak CG-based protection.
source: This reveals that those fragments for which we predict a minor role for CG density indeed display a strong shift in their methylation states while the ones where we predict CG density to have a major role only shift slightly.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the synthetic mutant library experiments.

claim: The amplitude of methylation gain upon removal of TF binding sites is related to the CG density of the fragment, resembling the prediction from the CG only model (R = 0.64).
source: Thus the amplitude of methylation gain upon removal of TF binding sites is related to the CG density of the fragment, resembling the prediction from the CG only model (Figure 3E, R = 0.64).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result from the mutant library experiments.

claim: Insertion of the high score REST motif leads to a loss of methylation while the low score motif has no effect.
source: Insertion of the high score motif leads to a loss of methylation while the low score motif has no effect (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the REST motif insertion experiment.

claim: Protein binding at regions with high CG densities contributes to a spatially constrained reduction of methylation.
source: Thus as previously shown for CG poor regions (Stadler et al., 2011), protein binding at regions with high CG densities contributes to a spatially constrained reduction of the methylation acquired by the inserted fragment.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the REST motif insertion experiment with reference to previous work.

claim: Mouse fragments derived from CG rich regions are maintained unmethylated by the combined action of CG density and sequence specific protein binding.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that mouse fragments derived from CG rich regions are maintained unmethylated by the combined action of two different mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined experimental results.

claim: Applying the 'CG only' model to predict methylation for all CGs in the genome overestimates the methylation levels for a large fraction of the CGs (R2 = 0.47).
source: Consistent with the results obtained with the inserted mouse fragments (Figure 3C), we found that considering only CG densities in the prediction overestimates the methylation levels for a large fraction of the CGs in the genome (Figure 4A, R2 = 0.47, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from applying the model genome-wide.

claim: >50% of CGs within UMRs show lower methylation than predicted by their CG density.
source: Indeed >50% of CGs within UMRs show lower methylation than predicted by their CG density (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genome-wide analysis.

claim: A model integrating the presence of DHS to predict hypomethylated regions outperforms and complements a CG based model.
source: In order to account for this effect, we attempted to define the quantitative relationship between protein binding and methylation by creating models that integrate the presence of DHS to predict hypomethylated regions. Such model indeed outperforms and complements a CG based model (Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from modeling with DHS data.

claim: Combining CG and DHS into one model explains over two thirds (68% genome wide and 60% at CG rich regions) of the methylation variations observed in mESCs.
source: Combining CG and DHS into one model readily explains over two thirds (68% genome wide and 60% at CG rich regions) of the methylation variations observed in mESCs suggesting that CG density and TF binding are the major determinants of genomic methylation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the combined model.

claim: CG density and TF binding are the major determinants of genomic methylation.
source: Combining CG and DHS into one model readily explains over two thirds (68% genome wide and 60% at CG rich regions) of the methylation variations observed in mESCs suggesting that CG density and TF binding are the major determinants of genomic methylation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: The regulatory principles derived from mouse ESCs apply similarly in other somatic cell types and organisms.
source: Similar modeling in different human methylomes (Xie et al., 2013) revealed that these regulatory principles apply similarly in other somatic cell types and organism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from applying the model to human methylomes.

claim: CG rich regions show little variation in methylation between stem cells and neuronal progenitors.
source: As a whole CG rich regions show little variation between both cell states in line with continuous hypomethylation of CGIs during cellular differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing methylation between cell types.

claim: CG poor regions experience extensive methylation changes across cell lines.
source: This is in contrast to CG poor regions that experience extensive methylations changes across cell lines (Figure 5B) (Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to figure and citation.

claim: Cytosines that change their methylation status during differentiation reside within fragments where a CG only model predicts a methylated state.
source: Interestingly, cytosines that change their methylation status reside within fragments where a CG only model predicts a methylated state, and little changes are observed within regions where an unmethylated state is predicted (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from analyzing methylation dynamics.

claim: The observed increased methylation during differentiation approaches the methylation state as predicted by the CG only model.
source: Notably the observed increased methylation during differentiation approaches the methylation state as predicted by the CG only model (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the differentiation analysis.

claim: Motifs for stem cell or neuron specific TFs are enriched around differentially methylated CGs.
source: Indeed, motifs for stem cell or neuron specific TFs are enriched around differentially methylated CGs (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from motif enrichment analysis.

claim: A methylation increase is observed in neuronal progenitors within CG rich regions at binding sites of the stem cell specific pluripotency factor Oct4.
source: For example we observe a methylation increase in neuronal progenitors within CG rich regions at binding sites of the stem cell specific pluripotency factor Oct4 (Pou5f1), while regions bound by factors expressed in both cell types such as REST do not change their status (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated as a specific example with reference to figure data.

claim: Regions bound by factors expressed in both cell types such as REST do not change their methylation status during differentiation.
source: For example we observe a methylation increase in neuronal progenitors within CG rich regions at binding sites of the stem cell specific pluripotency factor Oct4 (Pou5f1), while regions bound by factors expressed in both cell types such as REST do not change their status (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated as a specific example with reference to figure data.

claim: Methylation changes coincide with changes in DHS at CG poor regions.
source: We observe that the methylation changes are tightly anti-correlated to DHS changes at CG poor regions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing DHS and methylation dynamics.

claim: When DHS changes of similar amplitude are detected at higher CG densities, methylation levels do not change.
source: However, when DHS changes of similar amplitude are detected at higher CG densities, methylation levels do not change.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the DHS and methylation analysis.

claim: TF binding contributes to the unmethylated state at CG poorer regions within CGIs, while TF binding is non-essential within highly CG rich regions of islands.
source: These data are consistent with the model that TF binding contributes to the unmethylated state at CG poorer regions within CGIs, while TF binding is non-essential within highly CG rich regions of islands.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined analyses.

claim: The CG dependent effect is remarkably stable across cell types.
source: We observe that, unlike the TF driven effect, the CG dependent effect is remarkably stable across cell types.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing across cell types.

claim: Within islands, a subset of CGs embedded in short CG dense patches are unmethylated regardless of the binding by TFs in their neighborhood.
source: A direct consequence of this observation is that within islands, a subset of CGs embedded in short CG dense patches are unmethylated regardless of the binding by TFs in their neighborhood (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the observations with reference to supporting data.

claim: CG dense patches are absent in 50% of all CGIs.
source: Importantly however, these patches are not essential to form unmethylated regions, as they are absent in 50% of all CGIs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and only contain 30% of all CGs within islands.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genome-wide analysis.

claim: CG dense patches only contain 30% of all CGs within islands.
source: Importantly however, these patches are not essential to form unmethylated regions, as they are absent in 50% of all CGIs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and only contain 30% of all CGs within islands.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genome-wide analysis.

claim: For the majority of CGs (67.5%) within islands TF binding could contribute to their unmethylated state.
source: Thus our findings support the notion that CGIs arose as an evolutionary footprint of ancient regulatory regions. Such scenario is still compatible with a subsequent specialization of proteins such as CFP1 or KDM2A to recognize unmethylated CGs by CXXC domains in order to target chromatin processes to regulatory regions (Blackledge et al., 2010; Thomson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the quantitative analysis.

claim: Normal colon cells show methylation changes that follow the CG-based model.
source: This reveals that normal colon cells show methylation changes that follow our model, while colon cancer cells display a distinct hyper-methylation phenotype (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is stated as a result from comparing normal and cancer methylomes.

claim: Colon cancer cells display a distinct hyper-methylation phenotype that does not follow the CG-based model.
source: This reveals that normal colon cells show methylation changes that follow our model, while colon cancer cells display a distinct hyper-methylation phenotype (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is stated as a result from comparing normal and cancer methylomes.

claim: Cancer cells show significant gain in methylation even at CGs that are constitutively unmethylated in normal tissues due to their high CG density.
source: We observe a significant gain in methylation even at CGs that are constitutively unmethylated in normal tissues due to their high CG density (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from cancer methylome analysis.

claim: Cancer hyper-methylation at islands is mechanistically distinct as it cannot be modeled with the same local determinants that describe methylation changes during normal development.
source: This argues that cancer hyper-methylation at islands is mechanistically distinct as it cannot be modeled with the same local determinant that describe methylation changes during normal development.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing cancer and normal methylation patterns.

claim: The observation that cancer hyper-methylation affects both CG-driven and TF-mediated effects suggests it cannot be explained by alterations in transcription factor binding patterns alone.
source: Since both CG driven and TF mediated effects are affected this can unlikely be explained by alterations in transcription factor binding patterns.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the cancer methylation observations.

claim: The approach circumvents the limitations of previously used transient transfections which lack proper chromosomal context and are not controlled for amount of sequence variants per cell and their copy number.
source: It further circumvents the limitations of previously used transient transfections (Melnikov et al., 2012; Patwardhan et al., 2012; Sharon et al., 2012; Arnold et al., 2013), which lack a proper chromosomal context and are not controlled for amount of sequence variants per cell and their copy number.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method with citations to previous approaches.

claim: Only every second island harbors sequence stretches above the CG density threshold sufficient to create an unmethylated state.
source: Surprisingly, while we confirm that CG density is sufficient to create an unmethylated state, only every second island harbors sequence stretches above that threshold (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from genome-wide analysis.

claim: The higher the CG content, the lower the TF dependent changes in methylation and vice versa.
source: Our data argue that the higher the CG content, the lower the TF dependent changes in methylation and vice versa.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined analyses.

claim: The observed variability in methylation is not restricted to any particular location within CGIs but is only defined by local CG frequency.
source: Importantly however the observed variability in methylation is not restricted to any particular location within CGIs but is only defined by local CG frequency.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the spatial analysis of methylation within CGIs.

claim: It is not individual cytosines that are predictive for cancer, but rather the class of CGs affected as defined by the CG density model.
source: Notably it is not individual cytosines that are predictive for cancer, as these vary widely between types, but it is rather the class of CGs affected as defined by our CG density model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the cancer methylation analysis.

claim: Hypermethylation in cancer particularly targets CGIs that control genes that are inactive.
source: Hypermethylation in cancer particularly targets CGIs that control genes that are inactive (Gebhard et al., 2010; Berman et al., 2012; Sproul et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with citations.

claim: Hyper-methylated CGIs in cancer are embedded within larger domains of intermediate methylation (Partially Methylated Domains–PMDs).
source: Moreover, the study of cancer methylomes revealed that hyper-methylated CGIs were embedded within larger domains of intermediate methylation (Partially Methylated Domains–PMDs) (Hansen et al., 2011; Berman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous cancer methylome studies with citations.

claim: The observation that TF binding contributes substantially to hypomethylation at CGIs is compatible with the idea that the emergence of CG rich regions could have occurred indirectly through TF-driven demethylation and resulting reduced C to T transition.
source: The observation that TF binding contributes substantially to hypomethylation at CGIs has potential implications for their evolutionary origin as it is compatible with the idea that the emergence of CG rich regions could have occurred indirectly through TF-driven demethylation and resulting reduced C to T transition.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about evolutionary implications.

claim: There is limited positive selection for the CG content of islands.
source: This is in line with reports of limited positive selection for the CG content of islands (Cohen et al., 2011; Molaro et al., 2011) and that nucleotide composition including CG frequencies vary substantially between unmethylated regions across vertebrates (Long et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the evolutionary interpretation.

claim: Nucleotide composition including CG frequencies vary substantially between unmethylated regions across vertebrates.
source: This is in line with reports of limited positive selection for the CG content of islands (Cohen et al., 2011; Molaro et al., 2011) and that nucleotide composition including CG frequencies vary substantially between unmethylated regions across vertebrates (Long et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the evolutionary interpretation.

claim: The findings support the notion that CGIs arose as an evolutionary footprint of ancient regulatory regions.
source: Thus our findings support the notion that CGIs arose as an evolutionary footprint of ancient regulatory regions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the evolutionary origin of CGIs.

claim: The acquisition of methylation of fragments between different insertions was reproducible for most fragments between independent library insertions (R > 0.6).
source: The acquisition of methylation of fragments between different insertions was reproducible for most fragments between independent library insertions (R > 0.6) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a measure of reproducibility with reference to figure data.

claim: Around 30% of the initially inserted fragments are efficiently covered during methylation profiling, suggesting that bisulphite PCR is the limiting step of the experiment.
source: This reveals that around 30% of the initially inserted fragments are efficiently covered suggesting that bisulphite PCR is the limiting step of the experiment.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the technical efficiency with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
